svg.aria-label: Diagram: the structure of a Google Cloud VPC firewall rule as one direction, one action, one address family and one priority; why priority is the only axis that orders rules and neither target specificity nor protocol and port specificity breaks a tie, with deny beating allow only at equal priority and equal priority with equal action being indeterminate; the consequences of statefulness including the ten minute tracking window; and the TCP fragment gap plus the traffic no firewall rule can permit
svg.title: VPC firewall rules: one of everything, priority as the only order, and a fragment-sized gap
svg.text: A rule is one direction, one action, one address family — and priority is the only order.
Specificity never breaks a tie, in either direction — the same lesson as #69, a new subsystem.
The structure: one of everything
DIRECTION — ingress or egress, not both, and taken from the perspective of the TARGET.
Omit it and Google Cloud uses ingress.
ACTION — allow or deny, not both. FAMILY — IPv4 or IPv6 ranges, not both.
PRIORITY — integer from 0 to 65535 inclusive, default 1000. Lower number wins.
ENFORCEMENT — enabled or disabled, so a rule can be parked without being deleted.
And it belongs to ONE network: rules cannot be shared, not even across a peering.
Priority is the only axis that orders rules
Only the highest priority rule whose other components match is applied. The rest are ignored.
TARGET SPECIFICITY DOES NOT MATTER. A higher-priority rule for all targets beats a
lower-priority rule written for specific ones.
NOR DOES PROTOCOL OR PORT SPECIFICITY. A higher-priority allow for all protocols beats
a lower-priority deny of TCP 22 on the same targets.
DENY beats ALLOW only at EQUAL priority. Same priority and same action is indeterminate:
which rule gets logged is undefined, so use unique priorities if the logs must be read.
Stateful, and what follows from it
An allowed connection permits its return traffic, and you CANNOT deny that response.
Return traffic must match the reversed 5-tuple of the accepted request.
Tracking applies even to protocols that have no connections.
State stays active only while at least one packet is sent every 10 minutes.
So an idle connection can lose its tracking entry, and the return path with it.
The fragment hole, and traffic no rule can permit
VPC firewall rules do not reassemble fragmented TCP packets, so a TCP rule applies ONLY to
the first fragment — the one carrying the TCP header. Later fragments do not match.
Return traffic is the same story: tracking allows only the FIRST return fragment.
Beyond rules entirely: DHCP offers are blocked except from the metadata server; external
addresses accept only TCP, UDP, ICMP, IPIP, AH, ESP, SCTP and GRE; and egress to TCP 25
on an external address is blocked by default, with TLS on 465 or 587 excluded.
Enforced at the instance level, configured on the network — which is why a peered network
cannot borrow your rules, and why #61 found no choke point between subnets to inspect.
Two subsystems running, two places specificity does not decide and equal priority is a coin
flip. Priority is not a preference in either. It is how you refuse to let the platform pick.
